questions.title: Why does the Eighth Circuit limit penalty recovery under MPWA § 181.101 to the Commissioner?
questions.question_body: In Cohen v. Consilio, the court held that only the Commissioner can seek 'average daily wage penalties' under Minn. Stat. § 181.101, even though § 181.171 says an employer is liable for 'compensatory damages and other appropriate relief.' I'm confused about how the court distinguishes this section from other MPWA sections like § 181.13(a) where employees can explicitly charge and collect penalties. Does the court rely on the expressio unius canon here, or is there a specific administrative law principle limiting private enforcement of penalties in this context?

questions.title: Can a private plaintiff establish Article III standing to seek civil penalties payable to the state under Laidlaw?
questions.question_body: The court vacated the MFLSA claim due to jurisdictional concerns about standing for civil penalties payable to the Commissioner, citing Friends of the Earth v. Laidlaw. I understand Laidlaw allows citizen suits for penalties to deter future violations, but the court notes penalties here go to the state, not the plaintiff. Can someone clarify the specific test for standing when the relief sought (penalties) benefits the government rather than the plaintiff directly? Does the 'redressability' prong fail if the money doesn't go to the plaintiff?

questions.title: How does voluntary cessation of overtime policy affect mootness in wage theft cases?
questions.question_body: The court remanded the MFLSA claim to determine if the case is moot because Consilio paid the wages and liquidated damages. The opinion cites the standard that voluntary cessation doesn't moot a case unless it is 'absolutely clear' the conduct won't recur. Since the parties stipulated Cohen was paid, why isn't the case moot? What factual findings on remand would satisfy the 'capable of repetition yet evading review' or 'voluntary cessation' exceptions to mootness in this context?

questions.title: Does failing to cite statutory authority for penalties constitute waiver on appeal?
questions.question_body: Regarding the MWTA claim, the court affirmed the dismissal because Cohen 'points to no statutory authority allowing for civil penalties under this statute' and offered 'no meaningful argument.' I thought summary judgment appeals get reviewed de novo. Is this a waiver issue under appellate procedure rules, or did the court find the lack of statutory citation meant there was no genuine issue of material fact? What is the threshold for 'meaningful argument' to avoid waiver on appeal?

questions.title: Can a plaintiff raise new injunctive relief requests in summary judgment briefing?
questions.question_body: Cohen sought injunctive relief to rescind the overtime policy, but the court said the issue is 'not properly before us' because he changed the relief sought in his summary judgment briefing rather than amending the complaint. I know Fed. R. Civ. P. 15 governs amendments, but why can't you clarify or expand relief requests in opposition to summary judgment? At what point does a request for injunctive relief become procedurally defaulted?

questions.title: What is the procedural effect of a concurring opinion that vacates issues the majority affirms?
questions.question_body: The majority opinion concludes with 'We otherwise affirm,' but Judge Kobes' concurrence states, 'I also vacate the district court's ruling as to attorney’s fees, costs, and prejudgment interest.' As a student, I'm confused about the binding effect of this. Does the concurrence's view on fees become part of the mandate, or does the majority's 'affirm' control? How does the Eighth Circuit handle discrepancies between the majority judgment and a concurrence regarding specific remedies?
